draft.title: Other kinds of damages
card: Nominal
a very small sum that recognises the plaintiff's rights were breached, even though they suffered little or no real loss.
Contemptuous
a tiny sum, such as one cent, awarded when the court finds the plaintiff technically won but thinks the claim was worthless or the plaintiff has little to complain about.
Exemplary
a larger sum added to punish the defendant for very bad conduct and to warn others. It is not paid to cover loss.
These differ from compensatory damages, which aim to make up for the plaintiff's loss.
draft.remember: Nominal recognises a wrong, contemptuous shows disapproval of the claim, exemplary punishes.

a.q: Which kind of damages is awarded mainly to punish the defendant?
a.why: Exemplary damages punish the defendant for very bad conduct and warn others. Contemptuous damages are also tiny, but they show the court's low opinion of the claim, not a punishment of the defendant.
a.clue: The word exemplary suggests setting an example.

b.q: Sam sues a neighbour in Geelong for walking across his lawn. The court finds a wrong occurred but Sam lost nothing, so it awards one dollar to recognise the breach. What kind of damages is this?
b.why: A small sum that recognises a wrong where there was little or no loss is nominal damages. Contemptuous damages are also tiny, but they are used when the court thinks the claim itself was worthless, and nothing here says that.
b.clue: The court is recognising the wrong, not judging the claim.
